justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple modes, with wide vehicle lanes, a planted median, and a separate side path/sidewalk on the right, indicating some balance in spatial distribution for all users.
A continuous raised sidewalk or side path is visible along the right edge, which supports non-motorized users rather than dedicating the full corridor only to cars.
Accessibility is only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free details are visible in this scene.
Fairness is limited by the apparent absence of dedicated cycling infrastructure, so cyclists seem less well served than drivers on this corridor.
The landscaped median and verge improve order and separation, but they also occupy space that could otherwise support more explicit pedestrian or bicycle facilities.
safety: The roadway is wide and visually clear, with long sightlines and unobstructed forward visibility, which reduces immediate collision risk for drivers.
A planted central median separates opposing traffic streams, improving safety by lowering the chance of head-on conflicts.
Streetlights are installed along the corridor, suggesting basic nighttime safety infrastructure even though daylight conditions dominate the image.
The right-side sidewalk/path is physically offset from the main carriageway by a curb and planting strip, which helps protect pedestrians from moving traffic.
Safety is not higher because the broad, open road geometry may encourage higher vehicle speeds, and no visible traffic-calming features or crossings appear in the scene.
livability: Extensive trees and landscaped hedges create a greener and calmer corridor, which supports environmental quality for all road users.
The avenue appears clean, orderly, and well maintained, contributing positively to day-to-day urban experience.
Livability is constrained because there are no visible shops, benches, bus stops, kiosks, or active street-front uses that would support social interaction or daily convenience.
The street feels dominated by movement rather than staying activity, with a long linear road and little evidence of places to pause or gather.
Residential towers are visible in the distance, but the immediate edge lacks visible human-scale amenities that would increase street vitality.
sustainability: The corridor includes abundant mature trees and continuous planting in both the median and roadside strips, which support shade, carbon uptake, and ecological value.
Green landscaping along the roadway can help reduce heat buildup and improve stormwater absorption compared with a fully paved streetscape.
The presence of a separated non-motorized side path/sidewalk offers at least some support for walking, which is more sustainable than a car-only layout.
Sustainability is limited by the apparent emphasis on wide motor-traffic lanes and the lack of clearly marked bicycle lanes or visible public transit facilities.
The overall green-to-pavement balance is better than many arterial roads, helping the corridor perform relatively well on environmental grounds.
aesthetics: The street has a strong visual order, with symmetrical lighting poles, a straight corridor, and neatly maintained planting beds.
Large mature trees on both sides frame the avenue and create an attractive green canopy effect, especially on the right side.
Trimmed hedges in the median and verge add texture and visual refinement, making the roadway look cared for and cohesive.
The distant skyline of residential buildings adds depth without overwhelming the streetscape.
Aesthetics are slightly reduced by the very wide asphalt surface, which makes the center of the view feel somewhat monotonous and infrastructure-dominated.
comfort: Thermal comfort is reasonably good because mature roadside trees provide substantial shade, especially along the right-side path.
Physical comfort is supported by a smooth, even road surface and a continuous paved side path/sidewalk with no obvious debris or obstructions.
Psychological comfort benefits from the clean, spacious, and low-congestion appearance of the corridor.
Comfort is reduced by the strong direct sunlight and exposed central roadway, where users outside the tree shade would experience heat and glare.
No visible benches, shelters, or rest areas are present, so comfort for users who want to stop or linger is limited.
walkability: A continuous pedestrian side path/sidewalk is visible on the right, which gives walkers a dedicated linear route separated from traffic by curb and planting.
Tree cover along the edge improves walking comfort by adding shade and a greener visual environment.
Walkability remains modest because the corridor is very wide and auto-oriented, with long distances across the roadway and no visible crosswalks in this frame.
There are no visible benches, corner uses, storefronts, or active frontages to make walking more engaging or destination-rich.
The long uninterrupted road geometry suggests limited crossing opportunities and low pedestrian priority compared with vehicular movement.
bikeability: The street appears to have enough width to potentially accommodate cycling, and the smooth pavement would be comfortable for riding.
However, no dedicated bike lane markings, painted cycle symbols, or protected bicycle tracks are visible on the carriageway.
Cyclists would likely need to mix with motor traffic on a wide road that may encourage higher speeds, which lowers perceived and actual cycling safety.
The narrow side path on the right does not show signs that it is intended as a formal shared bikeway, so its suitability for cycling is uncertain.
No bicycle parking, bike signals, or intersection treatments are visible, indicating weak direct support for cycling.
